subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: An 80-year-old man presents with exertional syncope, chest pain, and shortness of breath. His radial pulse is weak and peaks late. Auscultation reveals a systolic murmur that is loudest at the heart base and radiates to the carotids, with a soft second heart sound.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this patient's murmur?

options.text: Holosystolic, high-pitched blowing murmur loudest at the apex and radiating to the axilla
Early diastolic, decrescendo, high-pitched blowing murmur best heard at the left sternal border
Crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur loudest at the base with radiation to the carotids, weak and delayed peripheral pulses, and a soft S2
Late crescendo murmur with a midsystolic click at the apex, loudest just before S2
Continuous machine-like murmur at the left infraclavicular area, loudest at S2

explanation_correct: This elderly patient has aortic stenosis from age-related calcification, presenting with the classic triad of Syncope, Angina, and Dyspnea on exertion (SAD). The murmur is a crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur loudest at the heart base and radiating to the carotids, with a soft S2 and sometimes an ejection click. 'Pulsus parvus et tardus'—weak pulses with a delayed peak—reflects the obstructed ejection through the calcified valve. Hemodynamically, left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure during systole.

explanation_incorrect.A: A holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla describes mitral regurgitation, which is not associated with pulsus parvus et tardus or the SAD triad.
explanation_incorrect.B: An early diastolic decrescendo blowing murmur at the left sternal border describes aortic regurgitation, a diastolic lesion with wide pulse pressure rather than weak delayed pulses.
explanation_incorrect.D: A late crescendo murmur with a midsystolic click at the apex describes mitral valve prolapse, which occurs in a younger population and is usually benign.
explanation_incorrect.E: A continuous machine-like murmur at the left infraclavicular area describes patent ductus arteriosus, classically due to congenital rubella or prematurity.

educationalObjective: Aortic stenosis produces a crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur at the base radiating to the carotids, soft S2, pulsus parvus et tardus, and the SAD triad.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 64-year-old man develops a new holosystolic, high-pitched 'blowing' murmur five days after a myocardial infarction. The murmur is loudest at the apex and radiates toward the axilla. He is dyspneic, and an echocardiogram shows impaired contraction of the papillary muscle region supplied by the infarcted artery.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's murmur?

options.text: Ischemic dysfunction of the papillary apparatus and left ventricular dilatation prevent proper mitral leaflet coaptation, allowing systolic regurgitation into the left atrium
Right ventricular dilatation from chronic volume overload pulls the tricuspid leaflets apart, allowing systolic regurgitation into the right atrium
Sudden tensing of the chordae tendineae as redundant mitral leaflets prolapse into the left atrium in late systole
Fusion of the mitral leaflet tips restricts diastolic opening, creating a pressure gradient from left atrium to left ventricle during filling
Rupture of the interventricular septum creates a left-to-right shunt that becomes audible as a continuous murmur

explanation_correct: This is acute mitral regurgitation after myocardial infarction, one of the classic causes—post-MI ischemic heart disease, mitral valve prolapse, left ventricular dilatation, and rheumatic fever. The holosystolic, high-pitched blowing murmur is loudest at the apex and radiates toward the axilla. Ischemic papillary dysfunction and ventricular dilation impair leaflet coaptation, so blood regurgitates into the left atrium during systole; infective endocarditis is also an important association for both mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.

explanation_incorrect.B: Tricuspid regurgitation from right ventricular dilatation produces a holosystolic murmur loudest at the tricuspid area, not the apex radiating to the axilla; this patient's lesion is mitral.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sudden chordae tensing with leaflet prolapse produces mitral valve prolapse, whose murmur is late systolic with a midsystolic click rather than holosystolic throughout contraction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Leaflet tip fusion restricting diastolic opening describes mitral stenosis, which produces a diastolic rumbling murmur after an opening snap, not a holosystolic murmur.
explanation_incorrect.E: A continuous murmur from left-to-right shunt flow describes a ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus physiology, not a post-MI papillary muscle mechanism.

educationalObjective: Mitral regurgitation is often due to post-MI ischemia, MVP, LV dilatation, or rheumatic fever, and is heard as a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 28-year-old woman has a routine checkup. Auscultation at the apex reveals a click in midsystole followed by a late crescendo murmur that is loudest just before S2; the click occurs after the carotid pulse is palpated. She is otherwise well, and her physician notes that although the condition is usually benign, it warrants attention in certain circumstances.
question: Which of the following best explains the click heard in this patient's murmur?

options.text: Abrupt halt of leaflet motion in diastole after rapid opening through fused leaflet tips
Turbulent flow through a calcified aortic valve as it reaches maximal opening in early systole
Sudden snapping shut of the pulmonic valve as right ventricular ejection ends
Pericardial rub from inflamed visceral and parietal layers sliding during ventricular contraction
Sudden tensing of the chordae tendineae as the mitral leaflets prolapse into the left atrium

explanation_correct: This patient has mitral valve prolapse: a late crescendo murmur with a midsystolic click (MC) best heard at the apex and loudest just before S2. The click is caused by the sudden tensing of the chordae tendineae as the mitral leaflets prolapse into the left atrium, and it characteristically occurs after the carotid pulse. MVP is usually benign but can predispose to infective endocarditis, and it can arise from rheumatic fever, chordae rupture, mitral annular disjunction, or myxomatous degeneration.

explanation_incorrect.A: An abrupt halt of leaflet motion after rapid opening through fused tips explains the opening snap of mitral stenosis, which occurs in early diastole—not a midsystolic click.
explanation_incorrect.B: Turbulent flow through a diseased aortic valve early in systole relates to the ejection click of aortic stenosis, which occurs before the carotid pulse and in a different auscultatory area.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pulmonic valve closure is the normal P2 component of S2, not a mid-systolic click associated with a late systolic murmur.
explanation_incorrect.D: A pericardial friction rub is a scratching, multi-component sound from pericardial inflammation, unrelated to chordae tendineae or the post-carotid timing described.

educationalObjective: The midsystolic click of mitral valve prolapse is due to sudden tensing of the chordae tendineae as leaflets prolapse into the left atrium, followed by a late crescendo murmur loudest just before S2.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 3-month-old infant is found to have a harsh-sounding holosystolic murmur loudest at the tricuspid area. The infant is feeding normally and growing appropriately, and no other abnormalities are noted on examination.
question: Which of the following best describes this infant's murmur and lesion?

options.text: A congenital defect with a continuous machine-like murmur, often due to congenital rubella or prematurity, that is loudest at S2
A congenital defect in which larger defects produce lower-intensity murmurs than smaller defects, with a holosystolic harsh murmur at the tricuspid area
A lesion producing a crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur that radiates to the carotids with weak, delayed pulses
A lesion producing a diastolic rumbling murmur that follows an opening snap and is a late sequela of rheumatic fever
A lesion producing a late crescendo murmur with a midsystolic click that is usually benign but predisposes to infective endocarditis

explanation_correct: This infant has a ventricular septal defect, the congenital lesion that produces a holosystolic, harsh-sounding murmur loudest at the tricuspid area. A key counterintuitive feature is that larger VSDs have lower-intensity murmurs than smaller ones, because a large defect allows low-velocity flow across a low-resistance opening while a small defect forces blood through a narrow orifice at high velocity.

explanation_incorrect.A: A continuous machine-like murmur loudest at S2 describes patent ductus arteriosus, best heard at the left infraclavicular area, not a holosystolic murmur at the tricuspid area.
explanation_incorrect.C: A crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur radiating to the carotids with pulsus parvus et tardus describes aortic stenosis, not a congenital holosystolic murmur in an infant.
explanation_incorrect.D: A diastolic rumble after an opening snap as a late sequela of rheumatic fever describes mitral stenosis, which is exceedingly unlikely in a 3-month-old.
explanation_incorrect.E: A late crescendo murmur with a midsystolic click describes mitral valve prolapse, a condition of older children and adults rather than a congenital lesion in infancy.

educationalObjective: Ventricular septal defect causes a harsh holosystolic murmur at the tricuspid area, and larger VSDs have lower-intensity murmurs than smaller ones.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 48-year-old woman with a remote history of rheumatic fever has a delayed, rumbling mid-to-late diastolic murmur at the apex. The interval between the second heart sound and the opening snap is notably short, and she has an irregularly irregular pulse. She is being evaluated to determine how severe her valve disease is.
question: What does the shortened interval between S2 and the opening snap indicate about this patient's valve disease?

options.text: Milder disease, because a more pliable valve opens later when left atrial pressure is only slightly elevated
The interval reflects the degree of left ventricular dilatation and carries no prognostic significance for the valve itself
Milder disease, because the valve leaflets remain mobile longer before fusing at their tips
More severe disease, because higher left atrial pressure forces the stenotic valve open earlier in diastole
More severe disease, because a shorter interval indicates that the aortic valve is closing earlier than normal

explanation_correct: In mitral stenosis, the murmur follows the opening snap, and a decreased interval between S2 and the opening snap correlates with increased severity. The opening snap arises from the abrupt halt of leaflet motion in diastole after rapid opening due to fusion at the leaflet tips, with left atrial pressure greatly exceeding left ventricular pressure during diastole. Higher left atrial pressure (worse stenosis) opens the valve earlier in diastole, shortening the S2–OS interval. Chronic MS leads to left atrial dilatation and pulmonary congestion, atrial fibrillation (her irregularly irregular pulse), Ortner syndrome, hemoptysis, and right heart failure.

explanation_incorrect.A: A late opening snap would occur with lower left atrial pressure in milder disease; an early (short S2–OS interval) snap indicates more severe stenosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: The S2–OS interval is a direct bedside marker of mitral stenosis severity through left atrial pressure; it is not a measure of ventricular dilatation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Leaflet mobility affects whether an opening snap is heard at all, but the timing of the snap within diastole tracks left atrial pressure, and a short interval means more severe disease, not milder.
explanation_incorrect.E: The interval is between the second heart sound and the mitral opening snap; aortic valve closure timing does not determine its length.

educationalObjective: In mitral stenosis, a shorter S2–opening snap interval correlates with greater severity, because higher left atrial pressure opens the stenotic valve earlier in diastole.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A premature infant born at 30 weeks' gestation has a continuous, machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area that is loudest at the second heart sound. The infant also has bounding peripheral pulses, and echocardiography confirms the suspected diagnosis.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the lesion responsible for this infant's murmur?

options.text: A holosystolic, harsh murmur at the tricuspid area from a defect in the interventricular septum
A late crescendo murmur with a midsystolic click at the apex from redundant mitral leaflets
A continuous machine-like murmur from persistent fetal circulation between the aorta and pulmonary artery, often due to prematurity or congenital rubella
An early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the base from a congenitally malformed aortic valve with two cusps
A delayed rumbling mid-to-late diastolic murmur after an opening snap from leaflet tip fusion

explanation_correct: This premature infant has a patent ductus arteriosus, which produces a continuous machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area and loudest at S2. PDA is often due to congenital rubella or prematurity. Because the ductus connects the aorta and pulmonary artery, flow continues through both systole and diastole, producing the continuous 'machinelike' quality and the bounding pulses.

explanation_incorrect.A: A ventricular septal defect produces a holosystolic harsh murmur at the tricuspid area, not a continuous murmur, and it is not the lesion associated with prematurity in this continuous-murmur pattern.
explanation_incorrect.B: Mitral valve prolapse produces a late crescendo murmur with a midsystolic click, which would not be heard in a premature infant as a continuous infraclavicular murmur.
explanation_incorrect.D: A bicuspid aortic valve produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur of aortic regurgitation, not a continuous machine-like sound.
explanation_incorrect.E: Leaflet tip fusion with an opening snap and diastolic rumble describes rheumatic mitral stenosis, a late sequela of rheumatic fever seen years later, not in a newborn.

educationalObjective: Patent ductus arteriosus produces a continuous machine-like murmur at the left infraclavicular area, loudest at S2, and is often due to congenital rubella or prematurity.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 34-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents with 5 days of fever and chills. Auscultation reveals an early diastolic, decrescendo, high-pitched 'blowing' murmur best heard at the left sternal border. Blood pressure is 150/40 mm Hg, and examination shows a pulsing nail bed and visible head bobbing with each heartbeat.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's murmur?

options.text: Age-related calcification of a tricuspid valve
Rheumatic fusion of the mitral leaflet tips
Myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve with chordal elongation
Right ventricular dilatation from a permanently placed pacemaker lead
Infective endocarditis involving the aortic valve

explanation_correct: This patient has aortic regurgitation, classically caused by the mnemonic BEAR: Bicuspid aortic valve, Endocarditis, Aortic root dilation, and rheumatic fever. Intravenous drug use is a major risk factor for infective endocarditis, which can destroy the aortic valve leaflets and produce an early diastolic decrescendo, high-pitched blowing murmur at the left sternal border. Severe chronic aortic regurgitation produces a wide pulse pressure (150/40) with hyperdynamic findings: pistol-shot femoral pulses, pulsing nail beds (Quincke sign), and head bobbing.

explanation_incorrect.A: Calcific valve disease causing stenosis is an age-related process of the aortic valve (over 60 years), not an infective diastolic regurgitant lesion in a 34-year-old.
explanation_incorrect.B: Rheumatic fusion of mitral leaflet tips causes mitral stenosis, a diastolic rumbling murmur that follows an opening snap, not an early diastolic blowing murmur at the left sternal border.
explanation_incorrect.C: Myxomatous degeneration with chordal elongation causes mitral valve prolapse with a late crescendo murmur and midsystolic click, not an early diastolic decrescendo murmur.
explanation_incorrect.D: Right ventricular dilatation related to a pacemaker lead causes tricuspid regurgitation, a holosystolic murmur at the tricuspid area, unrelated to the wide pulse pressure and diastolic murmur described.

educationalObjective: Aortic regurgitation arises from BEAR causes—bicuspid aortic valve, endocarditis, aortic root dilation, rheumatic fever—and produces a wide pulse pressure with hyperdynamic signs such as head bobbing and pulsing nail beds.
